atoms.b: After the Second World War, Britain experienced a major wave of ((immigration)) from its former colonies in the Caribbean. The people were invited to help rebuild the country. At that time, many hoped for full ((assimilation)) into British society, but nonetheless, they were still often met with prejudices.

Cities like London or Birmingham are home to large communities from South Asia, Africa and Eastern Europe. Some people warn that certain neighbourhoods have become ((parallel_societies)), where residents rarely interact with the wider British population. Instead of full assimilation, many sociologists argue that ((acculturation)) is a healthier model. It allows immigrants to adapt to life in ((the_West)) while keeping their traditions alive.

One of the most controversial police practices in Britain is the so-called “((stop_and_search))”, which allows officers to search people they find suspicious. Statistics show that Black people are far more likely to be stopped than white people, which many see as clear evidence of ((systemic_racism)). Activists from movements like Black Lives Matter UK argue that such inequalities are not simply the result of individual ((prejudices)) but are built into the institutions themselves.

Many young British Muslims, especially those of Pakistani or Bangladeshi heritage, grow up navigating a ((hybrid_identity)) — feeling British while also being connected to their parents' culture. Some experience exclusion and discrimination, which in rare cases can contribute to ((radicalisation)). Critics warn against reducing this complex issue to a ((one-track_mind)) narrative that blames all Muslims.
